out: Describe how AI and CI/CD fit into security operations.
plain: Automation is a dishwasher: it does one job the same way every time. Orchestration is the kitchen manager who coordinates the dishwasher, the oven and the staff so that a whole meal comes together.
tech: Use cases of automation and scripting include user provisioning, resource provisioning, desired state management (continuously correcting systems back to a defined configuration), anomaly detection and ticket management. Scripts, often using APIs, carry out the steps.

Considerations include guardrails, which limit what automation can do; automation logic, which must handle errors correctly; process engineering, as a poor process merely becomes a fast poor process; complexity; financial cost; process risks, such as one flawed run deleting many accounts; and deployment, including how changes are tested and released.

AI capabilities in security operations include agentic systems, which can take multiple steps towards a goal; chatbots, which answer analyst or user questions; predictive analysis, which forecasts likely issues; and AI-augmented baselines, which learn what is normal. Agentic tools need strict limits and human approval for risky actions.

Intended outcomes are efficiency and time saving, enforcing baselines, continuous improvements, productivity improvements, reduced downtime and increased proactivity. In SecOps, continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines build security checks into software delivery. Workflows combine automation with integrations between tools. Security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) platforms run playbooks that do this for incident work.

labs.title: Write a safe script
do: Create a text file that lists three fictional usernames.
Write a bash loop that prints what it would do for each one, without doing it. That is a dry run.
Add a guardrail so the script exits if the list holds more than five names.
Test it by adding a sixth name, and write a one-line log entry for each run.

What is the difference between automation and orchestration?
Automation does one task, and orchestration coordinates many tasks and tools.
lessons.title: Automation and orchestration
lessons.why: Analysts cannot manually keep up with alert volume. Automation improves speed and consistency, but a mistake in automation can spread instantly.
lessons.scenario: A SOAR playbook automatically isolates any host with a medium alert, and a false positive isolates a critical production server. What should change?
lessons.answer: Add guardrails: exclude or require approval for critical assets, and raise the confidence needed for automatic action. Automation should scale decisions only where they are safe.

product: Automation can disable an account in seconds, which is valuable until it disables the chief executive during a board meeting because of a false positive. Workflow builders need previews, limits and rollback, because the automation carries out whatever it has been told, at scale.

eng: What are the rate limits or caps on automated actions?
Can each automated action be reversed?
sec: Which actions may run without a person, and which need approval?
prod: Who should be allowed to create automations?

ex.title: Design a safe automated response rule
ex.scenario: An identity platform lets administrators build rules, for example "if impossible travel is detected, then disable the account". A rule recently disabled 200 traveling sales staff.
ex.problem: The builder has no preview, limits, approval or undo, so one bad rule can have a large effect instantly.
tasks: Design the rule builder's trigger, condition and action.
Design a dry run that shows who would have been affected.
Design limits, approvals for high-impact actions and a kill switch.
Design the run history and one-click reversal.
constraints: Automated actions must run under limited service permissions.
High-impact actions need rate limits, so a mistake can't run unchecked.
Every automated action must be logged with the rule that caused it.
needs: Security staff need a faster response to real attacks.
Affected employees need to know what happened and how to get help.
Administrators need to learn from mistakes.
ex.deliver: A rule builder, dry run, safeguards and run history design.

crit.t: Limits, logging and scoped service permissions are included.
The design considers a false positive at scale and the rule being misused.
The dry run makes the impact understandable before activation.
Automation is staged from recommend to approve to act, based on confidence.

seniors: Trust in automation is earned gradually, so offer modes that recommend before they act.
Consider who gets harmed by a false positive, as they are often not the person who built the rule.

cq.s: Which safeguard best limits the damage from a mistaken mass-disable rule?

a.t: A cap that pauses the rule after a set number of actions
a.w: This contains an error even when the rule was wrong.

a.t: A longer name field describing the rule's intended purpose
a.w: Better documentation doesn't limit what the rule does.

a.t: A monthly report listing every action taken by rules
a.w: A report arrives long after the damage is done.

a.t: Running the rule more frequently to catch problems sooner
a.w: This speeds up the mistake rather than containing it.

out: Follow the incident response stages in order.
Handle evidence with chain of custody.
plain: Responding to an incident is like responding to a fire. You prepare with drills and extinguishers, then detect the fire, work out what is burning, contain it, put it out, repair the damage and review what happened so it does not recur.
tech: Preparation includes training, testing, tabletop exercises (discussion-based walkthroughs), playbooks, simulation (practice using realistic scenarios) and assigning roles. Identification includes detection through alerts, internal advisory and external advisory sources and proactive threat hunting, which searches for attackers who have evaded detection.

Investigation includes digital forensics, chain of custody (documenting who handled evidence and when), e-discovery (identifying and producing electronic information for legal purposes) and preservation of evidence. Containment limits spread, for example quarantine/isolation of a host. Negotiation may involve a specialist negotiator in extortion events, working with legal counsel and considering sanctions and law enforcement guidance.

Eradication/recovery removes the cause and restores service. Notification/external reporting covers stakeholders, customers, law enforcement and mandatory reporting to regulators, sometimes within strict time limits. Post-incident work includes lessons learned, root cause analysis and post-incident reporting (PIR).

NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 now aligns incident response with the Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 functions instead of a separate four-phase cycle. Follow the stage names in CompTIA's objectives for the exam, and know that real organizations may use other models.

also.title: Detection and incident response in plain words

lessons.title: Incident response
lessons.why: Every organization will have incidents. A rehearsed response limits damage, and mistakes made in panic can destroy evidence or make things worse.
lessons.scenario: An analyst finds malware on a laptop and immediately wipes and reinstalls it. Which incident response problems does this cause?
lessons.answer: It destroys evidence before investigation, so scope and root cause may never be known and any legal use is lost. The host should have been isolated and evidence preserved first.

product: For users, an incident is a personal event: their account was used, their money moved, their trust has gone. The stages of incident response map to their journey: detection becomes a warning, containment locks the attacker out, eradication removes the attacker's access, recovery restores the person, and lessons learned change the product.

eng: Which sessions, tokens and devices can we revoke for one account?
What changes did the attacker make that we must detect and reverse?
sec: What must we preserve as evidence before changing anything?
prod: Who communicates with affected users, and what are our legal notification duties?

ex.title: Design account compromise investigation and recovery
ex.scenario: Attackers take over accounts in a personal finance app through reused passwords. They add new payees, change the notification email and create forwarding rules.
ex.problem: Support has a set of manual steps, and victims get no clear guidance. Sessions stay active and attacker changes remain after a password reset.
tasks: Map incident stages to the user journey and to the support console.
Design the "This wasn't me" entry point and secure lockdown.
Design the review of what changed: payees, email, devices, rules.
Design recovery and the follow-up communications.
constraints: A password reset alone doesn't end existing sessions or undo changes.
The attacker may control the email address on file, so recovery can't rely only on it.
Evidence must be preserved before accounts are altered.
needs: Victims are stressed, so they need one clear next step at a time.
Support staff need a complete picture of the attacker's actions.
Security staff need preserved evidence and patterns.
ex.deliver: An incident journey map and designs for lockdown, change review and recovery.

crit.t: The design ends sessions and reverses attacker changes, and it preserves evidence.
The design considers an attacker who still controls the email or tries to use the recovery path.
Language is calm, specific and doesn't blame the user.
Lessons learned feed back into product changes, with owners.

seniors: Avoid telling users that everything is safe until the investigation supports that statement.
Legal and communications must approve notifications, and the design should allow for that time.

cq.s: A user reports a takeover and resets their password. The attacker's device is still signed in. What was missed?

a.t: Revoking existing sessions and tokens during containment
a.w: A password reset alone often leaves existing sessions active.

a.t: Asking the user to choose a much longer password
a.w: A stronger password doesn't end the attacker's active session.

a.t: Sending a satisfaction survey after the case is closed
a.w: A survey does nothing to contain the attacker.

a.t: Deleting all the logs so that the account starts clean
a.w: This destroys evidence and doesn't remove the attacker.

out: Identify which log types answer which questions.
Choose suitable data sources for an investigation.
plain: Investigating an incident is like reconstructing a day using receipts, door badge records and security footage. Each source shows part of the picture. Combined, they tell the story.
tech: Log and trace data types include access and accounting logs, which are either logical (sign-ins to systems) or physical (door badges); device logs from network equipment; server logs; application logs; authentication logs; communication logs such as email or chat records; audit logs of administrative action; endpoint logs; network logs; and metadata, data about data, such as file timestamps or email headers.

Data sources include vulnerability scans, which show what was exploitable; automated reports; NetFlow and Internet Protocol Flow Information Export (IPFIX), which summarize flows; surveillance footage; security tools such as EDR; dashboards; and packet captures, which contain full traffic content.
terms: Logs from equipment such as routers.
Scan results showing weaknesses at a point in time.
Video recordings of a physical area.
Products such as EDR that record activity.
eg: A badge record shows someone entered the office after hours, and a matching logical login confirms which workstation was used.
Email header metadata shows the true sending server, despite the displayed sender name.

lessons.title: Data sources for investigations
lessons.why: In an investigation, the right data answers the question quickly. Knowing where to look is frequently what separates a two-hour triage from a two-week one.
lessons.scenario: An investigator needs to prove which employee physically accessed a server room overnight. Which data sources are most directly relevant?
lessons.answer: Physical access logs from badge readers, along with surveillance footage. Logical logs could show activity on systems but not who was in the room.

product: Audit logs are a product feature that customers buy. An investigator asks who did what, to which object, when, from where and with what result. If those fields are missing, inconsistent or easy to alter, the log is decoration. Export and retention settings then decide whether it survives until someone needs it.

eng: Which events are recorded today, and which are missing?
Can a log entry be modified or deleted by an administrator?
sec: What must be excluded from logs, such as secrets or personal data?
prod: What retention period do customers require by contract?

ex.title: Design an administrator audit log
ex.scenario: An enterprise customer is investigating whether a former administrator exported customer data before leaving. The product's activity page lists vague entries such as "User updated settings".
ex.problem: The log is missing actors, objects, old and new values and IP addresses, so it can't answer an investigator's questions.
tasks: Define the event schema: actor, action, target, time, source and result.
Design search and filtering, timeline view and detail with old and new values.
Design export and streaming to a customer's SIEM.
Design retention settings with their consequences.
constraints: Administrators must not be able to edit or delete audit entries.
Logs must not contain passwords, tokens or unnecessary personal data.
Time must be precise and shown with a clear time zone.
needs: Investigators need to reconstruct a sequence of events.
Compliance staff need evidence for a stated period.
Admins need to troubleshoot day-to-day changes.
ex.deliver: An event schema with examples, plus search, detail and export designs.

crit.t: Entries are complete, immutable to admins and free of secrets.
Insider misuse, including an admin covering their tracks, is considered.
A person can filter to one user and read a clear timeline.
Retention weighs investigation needs against privacy and cost.

seniors: Logging decisions are product decisions, because a missing event can't be recovered later.
Audit data can itself be sensitive, so decide who can read it.

out: Preserve evidence with hashes and images.
Use log-parsing techniques to extract a timeline.
plain: A forensic copy is like a photograph of a crime scene taken before anyone moves anything. Investigators work from the copy, so the original stays untouched.
tech: File and log integrity is confirmed by hashing a copy and comparing later. System images include a memory dump, which captures RAM; a bit-level copy, which duplicates every bit of a drive, including deleted space; and a snapshot, which captures the state of a VM. The order of volatility means collecting the most volatile sources, such as memory, before less volatile ones, such as disks.

Stakeholders include Human Resources (HR) for employee matters, accounts (finance) for financial losses and billing fraud, and legal for evidence, privacy and notification issues. Log-parsing techniques include filtering with grep, extracting fields with cut or awk, counting with sort and uniq, and using regular expressions, as well as queries in a SIEM.
terms: Assurance that files or logs were not altered.
A copy of a system's state.
An exact copy of every bit on a drive.
A captured state of a virtual machine.
Collecting the most short-lived evidence first.
Human Resources, involved in employee matters.
The finance team, involved in monetary issues.
Counsel involved in evidence and obligations.
Methods for extracting meaning from logs.
eg: An investigator hashes a disk image at collection and again before analysis. Matching values show the copy is unchanged.
A suspected insider case needs HR and legal involved early, to keep the investigation fair and lawful.

labs.title: Investigate a suspicious connection
labs.tool: grep, sort and uniq in your lab VM
do: Create auth.log containing these invented lines, adding your own: Oct 2 03:01 FAILED bob 198.51.100.7; Oct 2 03:02 FAILED amy 198.51.100.7; Oct 2 03:03 FAILED raj 198.51.100.7; Oct 2 03:04 OK raj 198.51.100.7; Oct 2 08:30 OK amy 10.0.4.15.
Run grep FAILED auth.log | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c to count failures by source.
Run sha256sum auth.log and save the hash. Copy the file, and verify the copy has the same hash.
Write a timeline and a one-paragraph incident summary.
Complete the log-analysis exercise under Performance-based practice in Atlas.
labs.expect: The counts show one source hitting several accounts, followed by a success for raj. The hashes of original and copy match.
labs.explain: One source failing against many accounts and then succeeding is the signature of a spraying attack that worked.
pass: Your summary identifies the attack, the affected account and the next action.

lessons.title: Evidence handling and hands-on log investigation
lessons.why: A good investigation needs both technical skill and care. Evidence that was changed can't be trusted, and a finding that isn't communicated to the right people can't be acted on.
lessons.scenario: A responder must collect evidence from a running compromised server. Should memory or disk be collected first, and why?
lessons.answer: Memory first, as it is the most volatile, and is lost at shutdown. Then collect a bit-level disk copy, and hash each item.

product: Legal holds and chain of custody reach products through e-discovery tools and evidence exports. A hold that can quietly be removed, or an export with no record of who ran it, undermines the evidence.

sec: Who may apply or lift a legal hold?
prod: Do customers need e-discovery in this product?
